snippet.title: Chip War, the Race for Semiconductor Supremacy | Full Documentary (2023)
snippet.description:
A new world order is taking shape before our eyes. The COVID-19 pandemic revealed the extent to which great powers depend on strategic products. The persistent shortage of semiconductors—essential to our daily lives—is reshaping geopolitical relations, fueling inflation and increasing tensions between the U.S. and China. 

It is estimated that 10 million cars worldwide were not produced in 2021 due to a lack of available semiconductors. From our computers to our toasters, from our tablets to our refrigerators, microprocessors, or semiconductors, power all our daily devices. They hold national strategic importance, supporting all advanced military and civilian technologies. Yet, while demand for both the quantity and quality of semiconductors has been growing, the number of places producing them has been shrinking. Only a few countries possess the specialized knowledge and capability to produce cutting-edge chips, with 63% of all chips manufactured in Taiwan. 

That this one island, which is already on the frontline of a superpower struggle between the U.S. and China, dominates production means that the world’s economies are dependent on the stability of Taiwan. So what can be done to secure microprocessors? And how is the battle for semiconductors already affecting our daily lives?

snippet.title: Chip War | Microchips, Global Chaos | The Hidden Tech Struggle
snippet.description:
A new world order is emerging, shaped by an unseen yet critical resource: semiconductors. These tiny microprocessors power nearly every aspect of modern life, from computers and smartphones to cars, refrigerators, and even advanced military technologies. 

Chip War
Year: 2023  
Duration: 52 minutes  
Production: Babel Doc  
Director: Nicolas Vescovacci  
Language: English  
Country of Production: France  

The global shortage of these essential components has exposed the fragility of supply chains, driving inflation, stalling industries, and intensifying geopolitical tensions, particularly between the United States and China.  

In 2021 alone, an estimated 10 million cars were not produced due to a lack of semiconductors. Yet while demand for these cutting-edge chips has soared, their production remains concentrated in only a handful of locations, with 63% of all chips produced in Taiwan. This dependency has made Taiwan not only the nerve center of the global tech economy but also a flashpoint in the ongoing power struggle between superpowers.  

Chip War explores how this reliance on a single island has placed the world’s economic and technological stability at risk. With Taiwan at the heart of a potential geopolitical conflict, the stakes could not be higher. This documentary examines the history, science, and strategic importance of semiconductors, detailing the efforts of governments and industries to diversify production and reduce dependency on a fragile supply chain.  

Through expert interviews and in-depth analysis, the film reveals how the semiconductor shortage is reshaping global relations and affecting daily life. From stalled car production lines to rising prices of consumer goods, the battle for microprocessors has already begun. But what solutions exist to secure this critical resource, and at what cost? Chip War provides a gripping look at one of the most urgent and complex challenges of our time.

snippet.title: Why China is losing the microchip war
snippet.description:
And why the US and China are fighting over silicon in the first place.

Subscribe and turn on notifications 🔔  so you don't miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO 

In October 2022, the Biden administration placed a large-scale ban on the sale of advanced semiconductor chips to China. They also implemented a series of other rules that prevents China from making these chips on their own. These chips are used in everyday technology, like our mobile phones and computers. They’re also crucial to military and intelligence systems, which is one of the main reasons they're at the center of a feud between the United States and China. 

Microchips were first invented in the US in the 1950s, after which their use rapidly expanded worldwide. Since then, the supply chain for these chips has grown and spread to include countries in Europe and Asia. And while some countries have caught up to the US's edge in making these advanced chips, China still falls far behind despite multiple attempts to gain an advantage.

Watch the latest episode of Vox Atlas to understand why China is losing a new cold war with the US over microchips.

Sources and further reading: 

We found this book written by Chris Miller very helpful for understanding the history of chip development in the US and the foreign policy behind its competition and feud with China: 

Chip War: The Fight for the World's Most Critical Technology
https://www.amazon.com/Chip-War-Worlds-Critical-Technology/dp/1982172002 

This book gave us great context on China’s efforts to acquire foreign technology: 

Chinese Industrial Espionage by Anna Puglisi
https://www.amazon.com/Books-Anna-B-Puglisi/s?rh=n%3A283155%2Cp_27%3AAnna+B.+Puglisi

Articles like this by Chien-Huei Wu helped us learn more about how much the US replies on east asian countries for successful technology:
https://thediplomat.com/2022/05/east-asian-firms-are-critical-to-americas-semiconductor-success/

Reporting by Bloomberg helped us understand major IP theft cases related to semiconductor chips: 
https://cset.georgetown.edu/article/engineer-who-fled-charges-of-stealing-chip-technology-in-us-now-thrives-in-china/

An excellent report for more detail:

snippet.title: The Global Semiconductor War Explained | World Lens Podcast (Episode 5)
snippet.description:
We built the modern world on tiny pieces of silicon… then quietly turned them into weapons of power.

In this episode of The World Lens Podcast, Mark sits down with our AI co-host Michael to unpack the real story behind semiconductors: who designs them, who makes them, who controls the tools, and why a handful of fabs and factories now sit at the centre of global power.

This is not a hardware review. This is geopolitics in chip form:
– Why microchips moved from “boring industry” to front-line strategic assets
– How the US, China, Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, Europe and others fit into the supply chain
– Why TSMC and ASML get mentioned in every “chip war” article
– What happens to AI, defence, finance and everyday tech if Taiwan or key fabs go offline
– The difference between “cutting edge” and “mature node” chips (and why both matter)
– How export controls, sanctions and blockades could weaponise silicon
– What a healthier, less fragile chip world might actually look like

This conversation is neutral and explanatory. We are not cheering for any side. We are walking through how power, risk and dependence really work in the semiconductor world – from gamers yelling about GPUs to militaries worrying about supply chains.

snippet.title: How Taiwan’s Semiconductor Chips Control the Economy | The Global Chip War
snippet.description:
The global chip war is reshaping international power dynamics and everyday technology. Understand how control over the semiconductor industry dictates the future of global economics and security.

From smartphones and computers to AI servers and cars, nearly every advanced technology depends on tiny microchips built on silicon.

But the global semiconductor industry is highly concentrated — and one small island plays a critical role: Taiwan.

At the center of this system stands the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s leading producer of advanced chips. Companies such as Apple, NVIDIA, and AMD design powerful processors, but rely on TSMC’s manufacturing capabilities to turn these designs into real products.

This video explains how semiconductors are made, why Taiwan dominates advanced chip production, and why microchips have become a central factor in global economic power and geopolitics.

snippet.title: The US-China Chip War is Over (And China Lost)
snippet.description:
If you look at the headlines, it seems like China is winning the semiconductor war. When Huawei released the Mate 60 Pro smartphone featuring a domestically produced 7-nanometer chip, shockwaves rippled through Washington. Armed with unlimited state capital and a history of reverse-engineering everything from high-speed rail to stealth fighters, it feels inevitable that China will eventually catch up.

But this is an illusion. Building a modern semiconductor ecosystem is not a problem you can solve simply by throwing billions of dollars at it. This video breaks down the two insurmountable walls standing in Beijing's way: The physical impossibility of copying ASML’s EUV lithography machines, and the invisible, absolute software monopoly of Nvidia's CUDA platform. It reveals why trying to catch the US and its allies in the chip war is like trying to hit a target that is accelerating away from you at the speed of light.
